copy.privacy.title: Privacy policy
copy.privacy.intro: This policy explains, in plain English, what the lanckrietchess Training Hub (the “hub”) does with your data. The short version: the hub is built to keep your training on your own device, and it only sends something to a server when a feature needs it or when you choose to share it.
copy.privacy.s1.title: At a glance
copy.privacy.s1.text:
- **No ads and no tracking.** The hub has no advertising, no analytics service and no tracking cookies, and it never sells your data.
- **Your training stays on your device.** Progress, streaks, games, mistakes and repertoires live in your own browser unless you switch on a feature that shares part of it.
- **Sharing is your choice.** The leaderboards, friends, the community ELO board and anonymous training stats are opt-in, and you can switch them off again.
- **What you type is used for what you asked.** A support question or an application goes to {coach} and nowhere else.
- **You stay in control.** You can reset your progress, leave the boards, disconnect your chess accounts and ask for your data to be deleted.
copy.privacy.s2.title: Who is responsible
copy.privacy.s2.text:
The controller of your data is Kyenzo Lanckriet (lanckrietchess), based in Middelkerke, Belgium. The hub is a progressive web app: you open it in your browser, install it on your phone, or open it inside the Skool classroom.

Because the controller is based in Belgium, the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and Belgian data protection law apply. You can reach {coach} through the contact options at the bottom of this page.
copy.privacy.s3.title: What stays on your device
copy.privacy.s3.text:
The hub stores the following in your browser’s local storage, on your own device. None of it is sent anywhere unless a section below says so:
- Your profile: the name or username you choose, your rating, main leak, goal, Hyper-Focus and check-ins, your struggles and your repertoire choices.
- Your progress: accuracy, streaks, finished drills, badges, mistakes saved for spaced repetition, your Puzzle ELO and your credits.
- Your games and positions: reviewed games, the Game Vault, brilliant moves, your own repertoires and your last Trim session.
- Your membership: the member key you entered and a random device ID that identifies this browser to the hub.
- Your settings, your friends list and the answers you gave in the Upgrades chat.

The hub does not use cookies for this. The profile token and the coach briefing in your profile are created on your device; if you copy them into another service, that service receives what they contain. Stockfish, the chess engine, also runs on your device and sends nothing anywhere.

Reset my progress in your profile removes your progress. Clearing the site data in your browser removes everything, and that cannot be undone.
copy.privacy.s4.title: What is sent to the hub’s server
copy.privacy.s4.text:
The hub can connect to a server run for lanckrietchess (the “Arena server”, hosted on Cloudflare with a database). It is only used when {coach} has switched it on, and only for the features below:
- **Leaderboards and tournament.** If you join, your chosen username, your rating bracket, your puzzle results and your scores are stored and shown to other players. Without a username you are not shown.
- **Puzzle ELO and Trim boards.** Your username, bracket, Puzzle ELO and peak, your rated puzzle results, and counts of games reviewed and blunders solved.
- **Community ELO board.** If you connect Chess.com or Lichess, the server checks a one-time code in your profile and reads your public username, avatar and ratings from that site, then shows them on the board.
- **Friends.** Your friend card (name, rating, weekly progress, Hyper-Focus, tournament score and your latest blunder) when you share your friend code. With the server on, friends who have your code can fetch your latest card.
- **Peer puzzles.** When you review a game in Trim, your blunders and mistakes can be staged as puzzles: the position, the move you played, the better move, the opening, your name and rating. Positions from the hub’s own repertoire courses go to {coach} for review, including the moves of that game. Other positions can be offered to other players as free peer puzzles.
- **Anonymous training stats.** Only if you agree: which drills you miss, where your games leak, what you ask the coach (with emails, links and phone numbers removed) and Trim results. They are stored under a random ID that is not linked to your name, member key or leaderboard entry. Reviewed games and positions can be included without names.
- **Membership.** When you enter a member key, the server checks it and ties it to one device, using your random device ID.
copy.privacy.s5.title: The AI coach
copy.privacy.s5.text:
The Pro coach, a paid-member feature, answers through an AI model. The same goes for the Growth Path assistants, but only if {coach} has switched them on. When you type a question, the hub sends your message and the recent conversation, the position on the board and the moves of the game you are looking at, Stockfish’s lines, the review of the move you are on, and a short profile (name or username, rating, main leak, goal, Hyper-Focus, struggles and repertoire) to the Arena server. The server forwards this to the AI provider, Anthropic (Claude), and your member key is sent so the server can confirm your membership.

The free coach does not use AI: its question buttons are answered on your device.

Please do not type anything into the coach that you would not want processed by an AI provider, such as contact details or health information. Anthropic processes the request to produce an answer, under its own terms and privacy policy.
copy.privacy.s6.title: Messages, questions and applications
copy.privacy.s6.text:
Some features send what you type to {coach}, or to tools he uses to receive and organise requests:
- **Support questions and timeline answers.** Your name, your email or Instagram handle, your message or answer, your rating, the answers you gave in the Upgrades chat and your membership level.
- **Mentorship application.** Your name, contact, a one-line reason, your rating and where it comes from, your Chess.com and Lichess usernames, your goal, your Trim leak and how often it came back, your Hyper-Focus and a short application note. It is only sent after you tick the consent box, and you see what will be sent first.
- **Links to Instagram, Skool or an application form** open in a new tab. What happens there is covered by that service’s own privacy policy.

These messages may pass through automation tools such as Make, Zapier or ManyChat. They are used only to answer you, to handle your application and to keep a record of it.
copy.privacy.s7.title: Other services you connect to
copy.privacy.s7.text:
Opening the hub makes your browser contact a few services. They can see your IP address and basic technical data such as your browser, device and the time of the request:
- **Vercel** hosts the hub.
- **GitHub** serves the course data file and its version information.
- **Content delivery networks** (cdnjs, jsDelivr, Google Fonts, Tailwind CSS and Font Awesome) deliver code, fonts and icons.
- **Lichess** supplies rated puzzles, and **Chess.com** and Lichess supply public profile data when you connect or follow an account. The hub never asks for a password for either.
- **Skool** hosts the community, the classroom and the memberships. It has its own privacy policy.

We do not control the logs of these services. The hub never asks for or stores payment card details: memberships are paid on Skool.
copy.privacy.s8.title: Legal basis and how long data is kept
copy.privacy.s8.text:
Under the GDPR we process data on these grounds:
- **Consent** (Article 6(1)(a)) for the leaderboards, friends and community ELO features, anonymous training stats, support questions, applications and the questions you choose to send to the AI coach. You can withdraw consent at any time; this does not affect what happened before.
- **Performance of a contract** (Article 6(1)(b)) for member keys: checking your key and tying it to your device so you get the membership you have.
- **Legitimate interest** (Article 6(1)(f)) for keeping the hub secure and fair, for example limiting requests, checking that scores are plausible and hiding abusive usernames.

How long we keep it:
- Data on your device stays until you erase it.
- Leaderboard, tournament, friend and rating-board data on the server stays while you take part. It is deleted when you leave the board or switch the feature off, or when you ask.
- Anonymous training stats are deleted from the server when you switch sharing off.
- Support questions and applications are kept for as long as needed to answer them and to keep a record of your application. They are deleted on request.
- The services in the previous section follow their own retention periods.
copy.privacy.s9.title: Your choices in the app
copy.privacy.s9.text:
Where to find the controls:
- **Profile, community leaderboard.** Join or leave the boards. Leaving removes you from the server board.
- **Profile, anonymous training stats.** Switch it off and what was shared is deleted.
- **Profile, chess accounts.** Connect or disconnect Chess.com and Lichess. Disconnecting removes you from the community ELO board.
- **Profile, membership.** Remove your member key from this device.
- **Profile, reset my progress,** and the delete options in your Game Vault and My repertoire.
- **Friends.** Remove any friend. Your own friend code only contains what you see on your card.
- **Settings.** Achievement pop-ups and spaced repetition can be switched off in your profile.
- **Your browser.** Clearing the site data removes everything the hub stores on your device.
copy.privacy.s10.title: Your rights
copy.privacy.s10.text:
You have the right to:
- ask for access to the data we hold about you,
- have inaccurate data corrected,
- have your data erased,
- restrict or object to the processing,
- receive your data in a portable form,
- withdraw your consent at any time,
- not be subject to a decision based only on automated processing. The hub’s scores, ratings and recommendations only steer your training and never decide anything legal about you.

To use a right, contact {coach} through the options at the bottom of this page. To find your entries on the server, give your username, and your friend code if you have one. If we cannot identify you from the request, we may ask for proof that the data is yours. We answer within one month.

You can also lodge a complaint with the Belgian Data Protection Authority (Gegevensbeschermingsautoriteit / Autorité de protection des données, www.dataprotectionauthority.be) or with the supervisory authority in your own EU country.
copy.privacy.s11.title: Security and international transfers
copy.privacy.s11.text:
Connections to the hub and its servers use HTTPS. Member keys are published only as one-way hashes, and a key is tied to a single device. The key for the AI provider is kept on the server, never in the app. No system is perfectly secure, and anything stored in your browser can be read by someone with access to your device, so please use a screen lock.

Some of the services above operate from outside the European Economic Area, for example in the United States. Where that happens they rely on safeguards such as the EU–US Data Privacy Framework or Standard Contractual Clauses.
copy.privacy.s12.title: Children and changes
copy.privacy.s12.text:
The hub is not meant for children under 13, and we do not knowingly collect data from them. If you are below the age of digital consent in your country (13 in Belgium, up to 16 elsewhere in the EU), ask a parent or guardian before you share anything beyond your own device, such as joining a leaderboard or sending a message.

We may update this policy when the hub changes, for example when a feature that uses data is added. The date at the top shows the last update, and a change that affects your choices will be made visible in the hub.
copy.privacy.contact: Questions about your data, or a request to see, correct or delete it? Message {coach} directly. He answers himself. Please mention your username in the hub so he can find your entries.

# The MSPC System [free] | mspc
## M, Move: read their last move | M, threat, check, hanging
- What did their move change? | Every move attacks, defends or prepares something. Name it before you choose your own move.
- The threat scan | Before every move: which checks, captures and attacks does your opponent have now?
## S, Specifics: what this position is about | S, loose, hanging, structure, king, plan
- Loose pieces drop off | An undefended piece is a target. Count the defenders of every piece before you move.
- What the structure asks for | The pawn structure tells you where to play: the break, the outpost, the weak square.
## P, Priorities: checks, captures, attacks | P, forcing, check, capture, fork, pin, skewer, mate
- Checks, captures and attacks for both sides | List your forcing moves, then theirs. Forcing moves first, quiet moves after.
- Take the initiative | A forcing move that gains time beats a quiet move that only reacts.
## C, Calculation: to the end | C, calculation, sacrifice, mate
- Calculate to the end | Follow every forcing line until the position is quiet, including their best reply.
- The calculation cutoff | Do not stop halfway out of fear or hope: the reply you skipped is the one that beats you.

think.title: The quiet queen move
think.brief: You're Black in the Caro-Kann. White just played 5.Qe2, a quiet move with a very loud idea.

stages.prompt: What did 5.Qe2 actually change?

options.text: The queen lines up with my king on the e-file, so my e7-pawn is pinned and no longer guards d6.
options.why: Exactly. e7 was the only piece covering d6, and now it can't move without exposing your king.

options.text: It prepares queenside castling and a pawn storm against my king.
options.why: Castling is a plan for later. Read what the move does right now: the queen is on the same file as your king.

options.text: It only defends the knight on e4 a second time.
options.why: It does defend e4, but that is the surface. The real change is behind your pieces, on the e-file.

stages.prompt: Tap the square White's knight wants to jump to.
stages.hint: Which squares can the e4-knight reach with check?
stages.explain: d6. Nd6 would be check, the only guard of d6 is the pinned e7-pawn, and your king is boxed in by its own pieces.

stages.prompt: Your natural developing move is 5...Ngf6. What is White's strongest reply to it?

options.text: 6.Nd6, and it is checkmate.
options.why: Checks first. d7 is blocked by your knight, e7 by the pinned pawn, d8 and f8 by your own pieces. Smothered.

options.text: 6.Nxf6+, a normal trade.
options.why: That's what you expect, not what White plays. Look at every check, not only the obvious one.

options.text: 6.Bg5, pinning the knight.
options.why: A decent developing move, but it misses the knockout. Checks, captures, attacks: in that order.

stages.prompt: Play the safe route. White's replies come automatically.

5...Ndf6.note: The d7-knight goes to f6. The d-file opens, so your queen now guards d6 as well: 6.Nd6+ would just lose a piece to ...Qxd6.

alt.e6: Also safe: the e-pawn steps off the pinned file.
alt.Qc7: Also safe: the queen covers d6 directly.

bad.Ngf6: 6.Nd6 is mate. The e7-pawn is pinned by the queen and your own knight on d7 blocks the king.

6...Nxf6.note: Recapture and you are out of the trap with a completely normal position.

7...Bg4.note: Pin the knight to the queen. White spent a tempo on Qe2 and achieved nothing.

debrief.t: 5.Qe2 put the queen on your king's file. That pinned e7, and e7 was the only guard of d6.
Your king had no free squares: d7, e7, d8 and f8 were all occupied by your own pieces.
Your opponent's CCAs matter as much as yours. Nd6 is a check, and after 5...Ngf6 it is mate.
5...Ndf6 opens the d-file so the queen guards d6. Calculate it: 6.Nd6+ Qxd6 and the trap is gone.

think.title: One pawn, two targets
think.brief: You are White in the Colle. Black released the tension with ...c4 and just played 9...b5 on the queenside.

stages.prompt: What does 9...b5 tell you?

options.text: Black is busy on the queenside and did nothing about my e4-e5 push.
options.why: Exactly. Black's bishop on d6 and knight on f6 still stand on the two squares a pawn on e5 would attack.

options.text: Black threatens ...b4 to win my c3-pawn, so I must defend first.
options.why: ...b4 is a plan, not a threat that needs an answer this move. Check what your own pawn can do first.

options.text: Black is preparing ...e5 to take over the centre.
options.why: ...e5 isn't on the board yet, and your e-pawn gets there first.

stages.prompt: Tap the square where one pawn would attack two pieces.
stages.hint: A pawn on e5 attacks d6 and f6. What stands there?
stages.explain: e5. From there your pawn hits the d6-bishop and the f6-knight at once, and d4 protects it.

stages.prompt: Which CCA do you calculate first?

options.text: 10.e5, an attack on two pieces at once.
options.why: An attacking move that wins material by force. Black can only save one of the two pieces.

options.text: 10.exd5, a capture in the centre.
options.why: Captures are forcing, but this one wins nothing: 10...exd5 and the position is level.

options.text: 10.Qe2, developing and preparing Re1.
options.why: A good move in a normal position. Here it gives Black time for ...dxe4 or ...e5 and the fork disappears.

stages.prompt: Play the fork and collect the piece.

10.e5.note: The fork. d4 protects the pawn, so capturing on e5 only loses more material.

miss.Qe2: A sensible move in any other position, but e5 wins a piece right now.
miss.exd5: That releases the tension: after 10...exd5 the fork is gone for good.
miss.Re1: Too slow. The fork is available now and it will not come back.

11.exf6.note: Collect the knight. Black gets a pawn back with ...Nxf6 and you are a clean piece up.

debrief.t: 9...b5 was a queenside move. It didn't touch the centre and left the bishop and knight on the squares e5 attacks.
Colle structure: once Black plays ...c4 the tension is gone and e4-e5 gains space with tempo. d4 supports the pawn on e5.
Attacks count as CCAs: e5 hits two pieces at once, which is as forcing as a check.
Calculate Black's best try: 10...Be7 11.exf6 Nxf6 and you are a piece up for a pawn.

think.title: MSPC drill: the smothered mate
think.brief: You are a piece down. The entire MSPC cycle on one position: read the move, name the specifics, list the CCAs, then calculate to the end.

stages.prompt: What does Black's setup tell you?

options.text: The king on h8 has no escape squares: g7 and h7 are his own pawns
options.why: That is the feature the whole combination runs on. A king with no flight squares is a mating target, not a safe king.

options.text: Black is threatening ...Qxb2 and you must defend
options.why: Defending is exactly the reflex MSPC is built to stop. Read the position first: your attack is faster.

options.text: Black's extra piece means you should trade into an endgame
options.why: Trading when you are material down just loses more slowly. Look for the forcing line first.

stages.prompt: Tap the square both your queen and your knight can reach.
stages.hint: Your queen sits on the a2-g8 diagonal and your knight is on g5.
stages.explain: f7 is the intersection. The c4-queen covers it through d5 and e6, and the g5-knight jumps there with check.

stages.prompt: Which CCA do you calculate first?

options.text: Nf7+, because a check with the knight forces the king to a square you choose
options.why: Checks first. Forcing moves narrow the opponent's replies to almost nothing, which is what makes deep calculation possible.

options.text: Qxc6, because a capture wins material back
options.why: It wins a knight and loses the game to ...Qxb2 and counterplay. Checks come before captures when the king is boxed in.

options.text: Rd1, because an attacking move improves the worst piece
options.why: Slow moves come last. There is a forced mate on the board.

stages.prompt: Play the forced mate. Black's replies come automatically.

1.Nf7+.note: Check one. The king must go to g8 — the rook on e8 cannot capture and g7/h7 are blocked.

2.Nh6+.note: Double check from the knight and the queen together. Only the king may move, and 2...Kf8 runs into 3.Qf7 mate.

3.Qg8+.note: The queen sacrifice. It is not a sacrifice — it is a deflection: the rook is dragged onto g8 where it blocks the king's last square.

4.Nf7#.note: Philidor's Legacy. The king is smothered by his own pieces.

debrief.t: The king on h8 is walled in by g7 and h7 — no escape squares means mate patterns are live.
Your queen owns the a2-g8 diagonal, the knight has f7 and h6, and the black rook on e8 is one square from g8.
Checks, captures, attacks — and here the check is the move that keeps every reply forced.
Four moves, every one a check, so no calculation cutoff: at each step there was only one legal reply to consider.

think.title: MSPC drill: overloaded defender
think.brief: You are a bishop down and the black back rank is one move from collapse. Find the deflection.

stages.prompt: What has Black's play left behind?

options.text: Black never made luft: the king on g8 has no escape square.
options.why: That is the weakness everything else builds on. Three unmoved pawns in front of a king are a wall and a trap at the same time.

options.text: Black threatens ...Qd1+ with a back-rank mate of his own.
options.why: d1 is covered by your rook and your knight. Your back rank holds. The question is whether Black's does.

options.text: The bishop on b7 is loose, so I should attack it.
options.why: It is loose, but it is a slow target. Look for something forcing first.

stages.prompt: Tap Black's overloaded piece.
stages.hint: Which black piece is the only defender of the rook on e8?
stages.explain: The d8-queen is the sole defender of e8. An overloaded defender is the first thing to look for once you spot a weak back rank.

stages.prompt: Which forcing move do you check first?

options.text: Qxe8+, deflecting the queen onto e8
options.why: Take the defender's job away by force. After ...Qxe8 the queen is standing on the square she was defending.

options.text: Nd5, threatening to jump into e7
options.why: Black simply defends. A quiet threat gives the opponent a move; the back rank will be repaired with ...h6.

options.text: Re7, attacking along the seventh
options.why: The rook on e8 covers e7. Checks and captures come before attacking moves.

stages.prompt: Play it out.

1.Qxe8+.note: The queen is forced to recapture: the king cannot take, and no other black piece reaches e8.

2.Rxe8#.note: Back-rank mate. The pawns on f7, g7 and h7 that looked like a wall were the reason the king had nowhere to go.

debrief.t: Black never spent a move on ...h6, so the back rank has been a standing weakness the whole game.
One defender (the queen), one entry square (e8), one open file — that combination is what deflection tactics feed on.
Qxe8+ is both a check and a capture: the most forcing move available, so it is calculated first.
Two moves deep, but you must see to the end: the value of the queen is irrelevant once the line finishes in mate.

think.title: Remove the guard
think.brief: You are Black in the Advance with 3...c5. Everything you have done is aimed at d4. White just asked your bishop a question with 8.h3.

stages.prompt: What did 8.h3 do?

options.text: It attacks my bishop on g4, and does nothing for d4.
options.why: Right. A move that attacks one thing and defends nothing else gives you a free hand. Your bishop has to move or take, so make that move count.

options.text: It defends d4 a third time.
options.why: Look again: the h-pawn only touches g4. d4 has exactly the same defenders as before.

options.text: It prepares g4 and a kingside attack.
options.why: Your king isn't even castled. Read the concrete threat first: it's aimed at the bishop.

stages.prompt: Tap the pawn this whole position revolves around.
stages.hint: Your c5-pawn, your c6-knight and your b6-queen all point at the same square.
stages.explain: d4. You attack it three times (c5, Nc6, Qb6) and White defends it three times: c3, the f3-knight and the d1-queen. Remove one defender and it falls.

stages.prompt: Which CCA starts the win of d4?

options.text: 8...Bxf3, capturing a defender first.
options.why: Captures first, and the right capture: after Bxf3 the knight is gone and d4 has two defenders left against your three attackers.

options.text: 8...cxd4, taking on d4 straight away.
options.why: Your bishop is still hanging: 9.hxg4 and you've lost a piece. Deal with the attacked piece and the target in one move.

options.text: 8...Bh5, keeping the pin.
options.why: Solid but slow. White gets time for Be3 or dxc5 and d4 is safe again. The initiative was yours to take.

stages.prompt: Collect the pawn. Check White's counterplay at every step.

8...Bxf3.note: The guard is gone. d4 now has two defenders against three attackers.

9...cxd4.note: Now take. The c-file opens and d4 is about to fall.

10...Qxd4.note: The queen takes: centralised, and a clean pawn up.

bad.Nxd4: Natural, but 11.Bxd5! wins the pawn back: White has just enough activity. Take with the queen and the extra pawn stays.

11...Nxd4.note: A healthy extra pawn in the endgame, and the knight hits the f3-bishop. This is what pressure on d4 is for.

debrief.t: 8.h3 attacked the bishop and did nothing else. A one-job move gives you a free hand.
Advance structure: d4 is the base of White's pawn chain, the square your whole setup (...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6) is built to attack.
Count attackers and defenders: three against three. Capturing a defender with Bxf3 turns it into three against two.
Calculate to the end, including counterplay: 10...Nxd4? 11.Bxd5! hands the pawn back, while 10...Qxd4 keeps it.

think.title: When Black forks first
think.brief: You’re White in your Colle-Koltanowski. After 10.Qe2, Black didn’t wait: 10...dxe4.

stages.prompt: What did 10...dxe4 change?

options.text: The pawn on e4 attacks my bishop on d3 and my knight on f3 at the same time.
options.why: Exactly. A pawn fork: unless you recapture, one of the two pieces is lost.

options.text: It only opens the d-file for Black’s rooks.
options.why: The d-file matters later. Right now that pawn attacks two of your pieces.

options.text: Nothing urgent. I can play Re1 first and take back later.
options.why: Then 11...exf3 wins a piece. Read what the move attacks before you follow your own plan.

stages.prompt: Apart from the king, only one black piece defends h7. Tap it.
stages.hint: Which black piece can reach h7 in one move?
stages.explain: The f6-knight. Trade it off and your Bd3 and Qe2 both point straight at h7.

stages.prompt: Which recapture keeps the advantage?

options.text: 11.Nxe4: it recaptures and offers to trade the f6-knight.
options.why: Right. After 11...Nxe4 your queen or bishop recaptures on the b1-h7 diagonal, aiming at h7.

options.text: 11.Bxe4: take back with the bishop.
options.why: 11...Nxe4 12.Nxe4 and your light-squared bishop is gone. The pressure on h7 disappears with it.

options.text: 11.Bc2: save the bishop first.
options.why: 11...exf3 wins the knight. A fork has to be answered with a capture or a check.

stages.prompt: Play it out. Black’s replies come automatically.

11.Nxe4.note: The capture that answers the fork and offers to trade Black’s best defender.

11...Nxe4.note: Black trades, and the f6-knight is gone.

12.Qxe4.note: Queen and bishop line up on h7. The threat is 13.Qxh7 mate.

alt.Bxe4: Also good: the bishop recaptures and keeps aiming at h7. The course line takes with the queen to force a concession.

12...f5.note: The only defence. 12...Bd7?? 13.Qxh7 is mate, and after 12...Re8 13.Qxh7+ White wins.

13.Qc4.note: The queen steps away from the f5-pawn and eyes e6 and the c5-bishop. After ...f5, e6 stays weak for the rest of the game.

alt.Qe2: Playable too. Qc4 keeps more pressure on e6 and c5.
alt.Qh4: Playable too, but Qc4 is more precise.

debrief.t: 10...dxe4 forked your bishop and knight. Read what the move attacks before you follow your own plan.
Only the f6-knight defended h7. Trading it turned your Bd3 and Qe2 into an attack.
Checks, captures, attacks: 11.Nxe4 is a capture that answers the fork and offers the trade.
After 12.Qxe4 Black had exactly one defence, 12...f5, and it left e6 weak for the rest of the game.

think.title: Attack first: the Meran ...b4
think.brief: You’re Black in your Meran. White skipped castling and pushed 9.e4 straight away.

stages.prompt: What did 9.e4 change?

options.text: White threatens e4-e5, kicking my f6-knight away from the centre.
options.why: Right. The pawn wants e5, and from there it hits your best defender.

options.text: It only builds a big centre. Nothing is threatened yet.
options.why: Read it as a threat: next move e4-e5 hits the f6-knight.

options.text: It prepares queenside castling.
options.why: Castling is far away. Look at what the pawn attacks next: e4-e5.

stages.prompt: Tap the square White’s pawn wants to reach next move.
stages.hint: Which square would attack your f6-knight?
stages.explain: e5. From there the pawn hits the f6-knight, and the c3-knight is what makes the push work.

stages.prompt: Which move meets the threat with a bigger threat?

options.text: 9...b4, attacking the c3-knight first.
options.why: Yes. If White ignores it with 10.e5, then 10...bxc3 11.exf6 cxb2 12.Bxb2 Bb4+ and Black comes out a pawn up.

options.text: 9...Qa5, pinning the c3-knight.
options.why: It pins the knight, but e4-e5 still comes with tempo against f6.

options.text: 9...c5, striking in the centre immediately.
options.why: 10.e5 attacks f6 before your central counter-strike takes effect.

stages.prompt: Play 9...b4 and force White to react.

9...b4.note: Attacks c3 before White can play e5.

10...e5.note: Strikes at the centre while White's knight is out of position.

debrief.t: 9.e4 threatened e5. Recognize the threat before making your move.
The c3-knight supported e5. Kicking it with ...b4 breaks the coordination.
9...b4 creates an equal or bigger threat than White's e5.
Calculate 10.e5 bxc3! to see why White cannot ignore ...b4.

WELCOME TO YOUR BLACK REPERTOIRE.

THE BIG IDEA: you answer everything with 1...c6.
- Against 1.e4 you get a Caro-Kann.
- Against 1.d4 you get a Slav or Semi-Slav.
- Against 1.c4 and 1.Nf3 you transpose into one of those two.

One move, one system, every game. That is the same principle as a good White system opening: less memorising, more understanding.

IMPORTANT WARNING BEFORE YOU START:
Even if your opponent is a "1.d4 player", he can answer 1.d4 c6 with 2.e4 and you are simply in a Caro-Kann. So EVERY student needs this course, not only the ones who expect 1.e4. Do not skip it.

WHAT THIS COURSE COVERS: the Caro-Kann only. The Slav and Semi-Slav are a separate course.

HOW MUCH TO LEARN: eight short lessons. Learn Lessons 01 and 05 properly - together they cover the large majority of your games. The rest you can look up when you meet them.

THIS COURSE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER FIVE.

The opening courses tell you WHICH MOVES to play. This one tells you what to do once the opening is over - which is where your games are actually decided.

A NOTE ON WHAT THESE ARE:
These are model PLANS, shown as complete move sequences from the opening into the middlegame. They are not annotated historical games. Where a plan comes from a specific game, the source books contain it in full and I point you there rather than reproducing it here.

THE SIX STRUCTURES OF YOUR BLACK REPERTOIRE:
1. The Advance French with the good bishop (Caro, 3...c5)
2. The Tartakower doubled f-pawns
3. The isolated queen's pawn, seen from the defending side (Panov)
4. The Meran queenside majority
5. The bishop-pair structure (Moscow)
6. The doubled g-pawns after Nxg6 hxg6 (appears in FOUR different openings)

HOW TO STUDY THIS COURSE:
Play through each lesson once. Then close the file and answer two questions: what was Black's plan, and which move made it work. If you can answer both, you have what you need.

THE HABIT THIS COURSE BUILDS: at move fifteen, name the structure before you calculate anything.

AT THIS LEVEL YOUR OPPONENTS PREPARE.

Everything in the first two courses stays correct. What changes is that you now meet people who know the same lines you do, and who have chosen their move order to make life hard for you.

WHAT THIS COURSE ADDS:
1. The critical tries in each variation - the moves a prepared opponent actually plays.
2. Move-order traps in both directions: the ones you must avoid, and the ones you can set.
3. An honest assessment of where our lines stand, including the places where strong authors disagree.
4. A second weapon, for when you need to step out of your own preparation.

A WORD ON HONESTY IN OPENING STUDY:
Every repertoire has soft spots. A course that pretends otherwise is selling comfort, not chess. Where our lines are only "fine" rather than "better", this course says so - because knowing which of your positions are worse is what stops you from over-pressing and losing them.
The move that makes the whole repertoire work. We prepare ...d5 while keeping the c8-bishop free - unlike the French, where that bishop gets locked in.
Let's begin.
Let's get to work.

THE TRAPS YOU MUST AVOID.

1. In the Advance, ...e6 before the bishop is out. This is not a small inaccuracy - it is the whole variation thrown away. You reach an Advance French a tempo down, and Lakdawala calls it a clear mistake.

2. In the Advance with 4.dxc5, spending two or three moves recovering the pawn immediately. Develop first. The pawn usually comes back on its own.

3. In the Tartakower, recapturing with the g-pawn. 5...gxf6 is a completely different variation with a different character and much more risk.

4. In the Panov, ...Nc6 instead of ...Nbd7 at the wrong moment, allowing d4-d5 with tempo.

THE TRAPS YOU CAN SET:

1. The delayed pin. In the Tartakower, play ...Re8 before ...Bg4 and let White commit to h3. Most opponents play it automatically and hand you a target for the rest of the game.

2. The delayed capture. Against 6.Qc2 setups and in the Advance with 4.c3, wait until White commits a knight before taking or releasing the tension. The same move is worth much more two moves later.

3. The queen retreat. Against system players, provoking a committal pawn move and then retreating the queen is a real gain, even though it looks like you wasted time. Students hate this - teach it explicitly.

THE HABIT THAT SEPARATES 1600 FROM 2000:
Before every capture and every developing move, ask one question: does this move commit me to something? If yes, can I wait one move and make my opponent commit first?

SOURCES: Sverre Johnsen and Torbjorn Ringdal Hansen, Win with the Caro-Kann, for the Tartakower or Korchnoi Variation and the Bareev; Cyrus Lakdawala and Keaton Kiewra, Opening Repertoire: ...c6 (Everyman 2017) for the Advance and Panov; Peter Wells, Grandmaster Secrets: The Caro-Kann, for the dissenting assessment quoted in Lesson 08.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT ABOUT THIS COURSE.

Nothing you learned in the Speedcourse is replaced. Every move stays correct. What changes is depth: you now learn WHY the moves are chosen, what White's best tries are, and what to do when your opponent knows the theory too.

THE THREE THINGS THAT SEPARATE 1200 FROM 1600 IN THIS OPENING:

1. MOVE ORDER. In the Advance, the difference between releasing the tension with ...cxd4 and keeping it with ...Bg4 decides whether you get a comfortable game or a slightly passive one. This course teaches you when to do which.

2. THE ONE EXCEPTION TO THE BISHOP RULE. Everywhere in this repertoire you develop the c8-bishop before ...e6. There is exactly one place where the opposite is right, and knowing it is worth a lot of points. See Lesson 03.

3. PLANS INSTEAD OF MOVES. From here on, most of your games leave theory around move twelve. What decides them is whether you know the standard plan for the structure in front of you. Lesson 09 collects them.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES OF YOUR CARO REPERTOIRE.

Most of your games leave theory around move twelve. What decides them is whether you recognise which of these four you are in.

1. THE ADVANCE FRENCH STRUCTURE (pawns e5 vs e6/d5, our bishop OUTSIDE the chain).
Plan: pressure d4 with ...Nc6, ...Qb6, ...Nf5. Trade the light-squared bishops if you can. Break with ...f6 only when your pieces are ready.
Do not: play ...e6 before the bishop is out. That is the whole variation thrown away.

2. THE TARTAKOWER STRUCTURE (doubled f-pawns, open e-file).
Plan: ...Bd6, ...Re8, ...Nd7-f8, ...Be6, ...Qd7 and play against h3 or with ...f5.
Do not: allow mass exchanges into an endgame. Our structure is a middlegame asset and an endgame liability.

3. THE ISOLATED PAWN STRUCTURE (from the Panov).
Plan: survive the middlegame, trade pieces, then attack the pawn. Blockade the square in front of it.
Do not: weaken your king to avoid the initiative. Sit tight - it fades.

4. THE SYMMETRICAL STRUCTURE (from the Exchange).
Plan: create imbalance. ...Ne4, ...b5-b4, or the ...e5 break.
Do not: assume it is a draw. Symmetry is not equality.

THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL HABIT YOU CAN BUILD:
At move twelve, before you calculate anything, ask yourself which of these four structures is on the board. Then play the plan. Most opponents at your level do not do this, and that is where your extra points come from.

SOURCES: Cyrus Lakdawala and Keaton Kiewra, Opening Repertoire: ...c6 (Everyman 2017) for the Advance, Panov and Exchange; Sverre Johnsen and Torbjorn Ringdal Hansen, Win with the Caro-Kann, for the Tartakower or Korchnoi Variation. OUR MOVE, AND THE HEART OF THIS COURSE.

WHY WE PLAY IT: we head for a French pawn structure, but WITHOUT the bad bishop. In the French, Black's light-squared bishop gets buried behind pawns on e6 and d5. Here we strike at d4 first, and our bishop still has g4 and f5 available.

WHY WE ARE FINE EVEN A PAWN DOWN - three concrete reasons, straight from the theory:
1. THE BISHOP PAIR. Swapping our knight for White's dark-squared bishop, as we just did, leaves White with knights against our remaining bishop in an open, French-like position - exactly where bishops earn their keep.
2. FORCING A WEAKNESS. If White insists on defending c5 with the pawn move b4 instead of just letting it go, his queenside pawns get permanently damaged and become a long-term target.
3. THE ...b6! PAWN SACRIFICE. In some versions we can even offer a second pawn with ...b6, ripping open the queenside files for our pieces - very similar to Benko Gambit pressure.
Whichever of the three shows up in your game, the underlying reason is the same: White spent moves grabbing and holding a pawn, so we are ahead in development and our pieces have easy squares. As Tartakower put it, the worst bishop is still better than the best knight.

The pawn returns and the position is balanced.

THE HONEST ASSESSMENT: this is equality, not an advantage. If you are playing for a win with Black, your chances come later - from White over-pressing to justify his early pawn grab, not from the opening itself.

AN HONEST ASSESSMENT OF OUR MAIN LINE.

THE CASE FOR: Johnsen and Hansen call this their favourite opening and give it their whole first section. Their argument is that you cannot get far here by memorising - you need understanding - which means your study time compounds instead of expiring when theory moves on.

THE CASE AGAINST: Peter Wells, in his book on the Caro-Kann, writes plainly that he lacks enthusiasm for 5...exf6. He is a strong grandmaster and his view deserves to be heard.

WHAT THE DISAGREEMENT IS ABOUT: we accept a slightly inferior pawn structure for easy development and a clear attacking plan. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much you value structure versus activity - and that is a genuine question of taste, not a settled fact.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU IN PRACTICE:
1. Do not steer for endgames. Our structure is a middlegame asset and an endgame liability.
2. Do not over-press. Many of our positions are equal, and equal positions punish ambition.

Our doubled f-pawns and White's queenside majority genuinely favour White once almost everything is off the board, so with pieces still on, use your extra open file and activity to attack. THIS COURSE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER THREE.

The opening courses tell you WHICH MOVES to play. This one tells you WHAT TO DO once the opening is over - which is where almost every game is actually decided.

THE PRINCIPLE: openings do not produce positions, they produce STRUCTURES. The Colle produces only five. Learn the plan for each structure and you will never again reach move 15 without knowing what to do.

THE FIVE STRUCTURES:
1. THE GREEK GIFT - the h7 sacrifice. Not really a structure but a recurring pattern you must recognise instantly.
2. THE ROOK LIFT - your rook swings to h4 and joins the attack.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - pawn on e5, knight support, kingside pawn storm.
4. THE ISOLATED PAWN - you play against it, or with it.
5. BISHOP PAIR VERSUS SPACE - the slow anti-Colle games.

HOW TO STUDY THESE GAMES:
Do not memorise the moves. Play through each game once, then close the file and ask yourself: what was White's plan, and what was the move that made it work? If you can answer that, you have got what you need.

Every game here was actually played. The commentary explains the PLAN, not the variations.

WELCOME TO THE COLLE SYSTEM.

WHY THIS OPENING IS PERFECT FOR YOU RIGHT NOW:
You play almost the same seven moves in every single game. You do not need to memorise twenty different openings. You do not need to know what your opponent plays. You set up your pieces the same way, and then you attack.

Most players your level lose games in the opening because they do not know what to do. After this course, you will always know what to do.

THE SEVEN MOVES YOU MUST KNOW BY HEART:
d4, Nf3, e3, Bd3, Nbd2, O-O, and c3 (only when needed).
That is it. Learn these and you have an opening for life.

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS COURSE:
- Lesson 1: The setup and the plan
- Lesson 2: The e4 break (this is how you win)
- Lesson 3: The bishop sacrifice on h7 (the knockout punch)
- Lesson 4-6: What to do when Black plays something else
- Lesson 7: The three mistakes that cost you the game

TIME NEEDED: about two hours. Then start playing it immediately.

THIS IS THE BIG ONE. Twenty complete tournament games, chosen because every single one lands on a position from YOUR repertoire - the same c3 Colle-Koltanowski lines you already studied in Cursus 1-3. Nothing here is a random "Colle game found on the internet." Every game was checked move by move against the lines you were taught, and only kept if it matches.
WHY A WHOLE COURSE OF COMPLETE GAMES?
Opening theory tells you WHAT to play. Model games teach you HOW to play it - what the pieces are actually trying to do once the book moves run out, which plans work, which plans look good but do not, and what a real opponent does when things go wrong for him. You cannot get that from a variations tree. You can only get it from full games.
HOW THIS COURSE IS ORGANISED - the same opening tree logic as Cursus 4, but far bigger:
SECTION A - The main line and the Nc6 set-up (5 games)
SECTION B - The Nbd7 set-up and the Re1/Rxe4 recapture (6 games)
SECTION C - The Reversed Stonewall, against ...Be7 and ...b6 (4 games)
SECTION D - The Phoenix, 9.b4 (3 games)
SECTION E - Colle versus Queen's Indian, when the Stonewall is not available (2 games)
Every lesson starts on move 1, exactly like the other courses, so ChessTempo folds everything into one giant opening tree. You do not need to remember which lesson is which - just play through them in order.
HOW TO STUDY: play each game through once at normal speed without stopping. Then go back and read the comments at the marked moments - these are the moves where a plan succeeds, a plan fails, or a tactic decides the game. Ask yourself before reading each comment: what would I have played here, and why? That single habit is worth more than memorising any of these games move for move.
A NOTE ON THE SOURCES: these games and much of the analytical detail come from Colle's own tournament praxis and from Cyrus Lakdawala's "The Colle: Move by Move" (Everyman Chess, 2013), reworked here into our own words and tied directly to the repertoire decisions from Cursus 1-3. If a game or an idea grips you, the original books are worth owning - full annotated collections go far deeper than any single course can.

WELCOME TO THE MODEL GAMES ENCYCLOPEDIA FOR YOUR BLACK REPERTOIRE.

This course does for your Black repertoire what the Model Games Encyclopedia already did for your Colle-Koltanowski White repertoire: it takes every structure you have learned in the Speedcourse, Intermediate and Advanced courses and shows it played out by strong players, usually with Black in exactly your seat.

WHY THIS MATTERS: a repertoire course teaches you the moves. A model games course teaches you what those moves are FOR. Watching a 2600-rated grandmaster nurse the same ...b5/...a6 queenside majority you are learning, or defend the same isolated queen's pawn structure from the Exchange Slav side, does more for your understanding than another ten lines of pure theory.

HOW THIS COURSE IS ORGANISED: by repertoire branch, in the same order as your existing courses.
Semi-Slav side: Games 01-02 - the Meran; Game 03 - the Anti-Meran (6.Qc2); Games 04-05 - the Moscow declined and the Anti-Moscow Gambit accepted; Game 06 - the Exchange Slav.
Caro-Kann side: Game 07 - the Classical Tartakower/Korchnoi; Game 08 - the Advance (3...c5); Game 09 - the Panov (5...e6); Game 10 - the King's Indian Attack.

SOURCES FOR THIS COURSE: Cyrus Lakdawala and Keaton Kiewra, Opening Repertoire: ...c6 (Everyman 2017), for every game in this delivery, since its "Index of Complete Games" is built almost entirely from Alexey Dreev's and Igor Khenkin's own tournament praxis in exactly this repertoire.

A NOTE ON ACCURACY: the ...c6 sourcebook survives only as a heavily degraded OCR scan - the original figurine piece symbols are gone, replaced by near-random Latin characters, which is a worse starting point than the source books used for your White model games course. Every game in this course has therefore been cross-checked move by move with python-chess for legality, and where a middlegame or endgame passage could not be reconstructed with full confidence from the scan, the game is presented as a verified opening-to-middlegame excerpt with an honest note on how the rest unfolded, rather than a guessed-at move sequence. You will never be shown a move that has not been confirmed legal and consistent with the source. Two games (06, Exchange Slav; and the ...a6-first note in Game 03) diverge slightly from your repertoire's exact move order in the source material; both are flagged transparently at the point of difference rather than silently altered.

STILL TO COME: the Catalan set-up (5.g3), the London/Colle/Torre systems, the Reti and the English on the Semi-Slav side; the Two Knights and Fantasy Variation sidelines on the Caro-Kann side; and the Moscow & Anti-Moscow monograph has not yet been mined for additional games beyond Game 05. These are lower-frequency branches of your repertoire and are flagged here as the natural next expansion pass, exactly as Koltanowski's uncatalogued games were for the White course.

YOU ALREADY KNOW THE SETUP. This course is about the part that actually decides games: knowing WHICH plan fits WHICH structure, and when to switch.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES THIS OPENING PRODUCES:
1. ISOLATED QUEEN'S PAWN (IQP) - after e4 and the exchanges. You attack; you must not let the game reach a simple endgame.
2. HANGING PAWNS c4/d4 - more space, but two pawns to defend. Push d4-d5 at the right moment.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - after Ne5 and f4. You attack on the kingside with g4; Black counters on the queenside.
4. BISHOP PAIR VS SPACE - the anti-Colle lines with h3 and g4. Slow, positional, and your two bishops decide the endgame.

THE ONE DECISION THAT MATTERS MOST:
Does e4 work, or not?
- Black plays ...Nc6 and ...c5 → dxc5 first, then e4. (Lessons 01-06)
- Black plays ...Nbd7 → Re1 first, then e4, and take with the ROOK. (Lessons 07-08)
- Black plays ...b6 and ...Bb7, or a very solid ...Be7 → e4 is blunted. Switch to Ne5 and f4. (Lessons 09-10)

WHAT CHANGED SINCE THE SPEEDCOURSE:
Your opponents now defend. They will play ...h6 to stop the sacrifice, or trade pieces to kill your attack. This course teaches you what to do when the knockout punch is not available - which is most games from here on.

THE FORK IN THE ROAD. Everything up to here stays exactly as you already know it. Only move nine changes.

WEAPON 1: 9.e4 - the classical Koltanowski. Direct, attacking, and what you have played until now.
WEAPON 2: 9.b4 - the Phoenix. Positional, and objectively the harder nut for a prepared opponent.

WHY YOU NOW NEED A SECOND WEAPON:
Against accurate defence, 9.e4 gives White very little. Lessons 01 to 03 show you exactly where and how strong players neutralise it. That is not a reason to abandon 9.e4 - below 1800 it still scores heavily - but you should know its limits rather than discover them in a tournament.

WHAT 9.b4 ACTUALLY IS:
A Semi-Slav with colours reversed and a tempo extra. That framing, which comes from Lakdawala, is the most useful thing to know about it. If you have ever played or faced the Semi-Slav, you already understand the plans: expand on the queenside, break with c3-c4, and use the majority.

THE CATCH, and be honest about it: your extra tempo is Bd3, and that bishop can become a target for ...e5-e4 and ...Ng4-e5. The tempo is not free.

HOW TO CHOOSE AT THE BOARD:
- Opponent unknown or under 1800 → 9.e4. Play for the attack.
- Opponent clearly prepared, or plays 9...Qc7 and 10...h6 confidently → 9.b4. Take him out of book into a slow game.
- You need a win with less risk → 9.b4. The structures are unbalanced without being sharp.

THE DECISION POINT. Here is how to think about it.

PLAY 9.e4 WHEN:
- Your opponent is under roughly 1800, or unknown.
- He has already played a slightly passive move (...Be7, ...Re8 early, ...Nbd7 setups).
- You want a sharp game and the initiative.
- You need to win and are willing to take some risk.

PLAY 9.b4 WHEN:
- Your opponent looks prepared, or confidently answers 9.e4 Qc7 10.Qe2 with 10...h6.
- You want an unbalanced game with less concrete risk.
- You are the stronger player and want a long game with many chances to outplay him.
- You are facing someone who has clearly studied your games. This is your surprise weapon - use it sparingly and it stays one.

A WORD OF CAUTION ON REPERTOIRE BUILDING:
Do not try to play both in the same tournament game. Decide before you sit down. The worst outcome is knowing two systems shallowly instead of one deeply.

My recommendation for most students: master 9.e4 completely first. Add 9.b4 only once you are consistently reaching the middlegames from Lessons 01 to 03 and finding them unsatisfying. That is the signal you have outgrown the classical line - and not a day before.

- Cyrus Lakdawala, The Colle: Move by Move (Everyman 2013) for the 9.b4 Phoenix treatment and the reversed Semi-Slav framing.
- George Koltanowski, The Colle System, for the original plans and the advice to switch plans when the position asks for it.

WHY YOU NOW NEED A SECOND WEAPON:
Against accurate defence, 9.e4 gives White very little - even a 2660-rated grandmaster (Mamedyarov) once drifted into nothing with it against Volokitin at the 2004 Calvia Olympiad. Lessons 01 to 03 show you exactly where and how strong players neutralise 9.e4, and just as importantly, exactly where White can still fight back with precise play. That is not a reason to abandon 9.e4 - below 1800 it still scores heavily - but you should know its limits rather than discover them in a tournament.
WHAT 9.b4 ACTUALLY IS:
A Semi-Slav with colours reversed and a tempo extra. That framing, which comes from Lakdawala, is the most useful thing to know about it. If you have ever played or faced the Semi-Slav, you already understand the plans: expand on the queenside, break with c3-c4, and use the majority. Lakdawala notes there are hardly any games in the database with this exact plan - virtually every opponent you face will be entering the position for the first time in their life.
THE CATCH, and be honest about it: your extra tempo is Bd3, and that bishop can become a target for ...e5-e4 and ...Ng4-e5. The tempo is not free.
HOW TO CHOOSE AT THE BOARD:
- Opponent unknown or under 1800 → 9.e4. Play for the attack.
- Opponent clearly prepared, or plays 9...Qc7 and 10...h6 confidently → 9.b4. Take him out of book into a slow game.
- You need a win with less risk → 9.b4. The structures are unbalanced without being sharp.

THE DECISION POINT. Here is how to think about it.
PLAY 9.e4 WHEN:
- Your opponent is under roughly 1800, or unknown.
- He has already played a slightly passive move (...Be7, ...Re8 early, ...Nbd7 setups).
- You want a sharp game and the initiative.
- You need to win and are willing to take some risk.
PLAY 9.b4 WHEN:
- Your opponent looks prepared, or confidently answers 9.e4 Qc7 10.Qe2 with 10...h6.
- You want an unbalanced game with less concrete risk.
- You are the stronger player and want a long game with many chances to outplay him.
- You are facing someone who has clearly studied your games. This is your surprise weapon - use it sparingly and it stays one.
A WORD OF CAUTION ON REPERTOIRE BUILDING:
Do not try to play both in the same tournament game. Decide before you sit down. The worst outcome is knowing two systems shallowly instead of one deeply.
My recommendation for most students: master 9.e4 completely first, including the critical 10...h6 tests from Lessons 01-03. Add 9.b4 only once you are consistently reaching the middlegames from those lessons and finding them unsatisfying. That is the signal you have outgrown the classical line - and not a day before.
A FINAL PRACTICAL NOTE FOR GM-LEVEL PREPARATION: both weapons share the same first eight moves. This means your opening preparation time is not split in two - you are always in known territory until move nine, and only then do you decide which game you actually want to play. Very few amateur repertoires offer this much flexibility for this little extra memorisation.

- If Black's light-squared bishop is already outside the pawn chain (on g4 or f5), do not play Bd3. Play c4 or h3 instead.

WHY MOVE ORDERS MATTER AT YOUR LEVEL:
1. They let you steer opponents into positions you know.
2. They stop opponents from steering YOU into positions you do not.

THE THREE RULES THAT COVER ALMOST EVERYTHING:
- If Black's light-squared bishop is already outside the pawn chain (on g4 or f5), do not play Bd3. Play c4 or h3 instead.
- If Black has not played ...c5, do not play c3. Play e4 straight away.
- If Black has played ...b6 and ...Bb7, or ...g6 and ...Bg7, forget e4 and think about Ne5 and f4 - except against the fianchetto, where you play in the centre instead.

Learn those three and you will almost never be out of book, whatever your opponent tries.

SECTION D, the Advanced-level weapon from Cursus 3: 9.b4, nicknamed the Phoenix. THE CORE IDEA, worth understanding before a single move is played: the position White reaches here is a real Semi-Slav structure (1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nc3 Nbd7 6.Bd3 dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5) with Black's side of the board - but with an extra developing move already banked, since the bishop is already sitting on d6 instead of needing a tempo to get there. Study a handful of genuine Semi-Slav games with either colour and this whole structure will feel instantly familiar.

THE FORK IN THE ROAD. Everything up to here stays exactly as you already know it. Only move nine changes.

WEAPON 1: 9.e4 - the classical Koltanowski. Direct, attacking, and what you have played until now.
WEAPON 2: 9.b4 - the Phoenix. Positional, and objectively the harder nut for a prepared opponent.

WHY YOU NOW NEED A SECOND WEAPON:
Against accurate defence, 9.e4 gives White very little. Lessons 01 to 03 show you exactly where and how strong players neutralise it. That is not a reason to abandon 9.e4 - below 1800 it still scores heavily - but you should know its limits rather than discover them in a tournament.

WHAT 9.b4 ACTUALLY IS:
A Semi-Slav with colours reversed and a tempo extra. That framing, which comes from Lakdawala, is the most useful thing to know about it. If you have ever played or faced the Semi-Slav, you already understand the plans: expand on the queenside, break with c3-c4, and use the majority.

THE CATCH, and be honest about it: your extra tempo is Bd3, and that bishop can become a target for ...e5-e4 and ...Ng4-e5. The tempo is not free.

HOW TO CHOOSE AT THE BOARD:
- Opponent unknown or under 1800 → 9.e4. Play for the attack.
- Opponent clearly prepared, or plays 9...Qc7 and 10...h6 confidently → 9.b4. Take him out of book into a slow game.
- You need a win with less risk → 9.b4. The structures are unbalanced without being sharp.

THE DECISION POINT. Here is how to think about it.

PLAY 9.e4 WHEN:
- Your opponent is under roughly 1800, or unknown.
- He has already played a slightly passive move (...Be7, ...Re8 early, ...Nbd7 setups).
- You want a sharp game and the initiative.
- You need to win and are willing to take some risk.

PLAY 9.b4 WHEN:
- Your opponent looks prepared, or confidently answers 9.e4 Qc7 10.Qe2 with 10...h6.
- You want an unbalanced game with less concrete risk.
- You are the stronger player and want a long game with many chances to outplay him.
- You are facing someone who has clearly studied your games. This is your surprise weapon - use it sparingly and it stays one.

A WORD OF CAUTION ON REPERTOIRE BUILDING:
Do not try to play both in the same tournament game. Decide before you sit down. The worst outcome is knowing two systems shallowly instead of one deeply.

My recommendation for most students: master 9.e4 completely first. Add 9.b4 only once you are consistently reaching the middlegames from Lessons 01 to 03 and finding them unsatisfying. That is the signal you have outgrown the classical line - and not a day before.

THIS COURSE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER THREE.

The opening courses tell you WHICH MOVES to play. This one tells you WHAT TO DO once the opening is over - which is where almost every game is actually decided.

THE PRINCIPLE: openings do not produce positions, they produce STRUCTURES. The Colle produces only five. Learn the plan for each structure and you will never again reach move 15 without knowing what to do.

THE FIVE STRUCTURES:
1. THE GREEK GIFT - the h7 sacrifice. Not really a structure but a recurring pattern you must recognise instantly.
2. THE ROOK LIFT - your rook swings to h4 and joins the attack.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - pawn on e5, knight support, kingside pawn storm.
4. THE ISOLATED PAWN - you play against it, or with it.
5. BISHOP PAIR VERSUS SPACE - the slow anti-Colle games.

HOW TO STUDY THESE GAMES:
Do not memorise the moves. Play through each game once, then close the file and ask yourself: what was White's plan, and what was the move that made it work? If you can answer that, you have got what you need.

Every game here was actually played. The commentary explains the PLAN, not the variations.

THE FIVE RECURRING DECISIONS OF YOUR BLACK REPERTOIRE.

Almost every game you play with 1...c6 comes down to one of these. Learn to recognise them and you will rarely be without a plan.

DECISION 1 - WHERE DOES THE LIGHT-SQUARED BISHOP GO?
Default: out to f5 or g4 BEFORE ...e6.
Exception A: the Semi-Slav proper, where we accept a shut-in bishop because ...dxc4 and ...b5 pay for it.
Exception B: the English move order with 4.Nc3 Nbd7, where ...Bf5 runs into cxd5 and Qb3.
Exception C: against 4.Ne2 in the Advance, where White's own knight clogs his position.
The rule is not "always ...Bf5". It is: only bury the bishop if you are being paid for it.

DECISION 2 - WHEN DO WE TAKE ON c4?
Only when the recapture suits us. Against 6.Qc2 the same capture is bad on move six and excellent on move eight, because by then the bishop must recapture instead of a pawn.

DECISION 3 - WHEN DO WE BREAK WITH ...c5?
Only once it is supported: ...a6, ...b4 or a rook on c8 first. An unprepared ...c5 is met by d4-d5 with tempo.

DECISION 4 - DO WE ACCEPT THE PAWN?
Advance 4.dxc5: develop first, take later.
Catalan 5.g3: take it, but give it back for development when the moment comes.
Moscow 6.Bh4: only if you have studied the gambit properly.

DECISION 5 - MIDDLEGAME OR ENDGAME?
Tartakower: keep queens on. Our structure is a middlegame asset.
Moscow: patient - the bishop pair does not expire.
Panov: trade pieces. The isolated pawn gets weaker with every exchange.

THE HABIT: at move fifteen, name the structure and name the decision in front of you. Then play.

SOURCES: Cyrus Lakdawala and Keaton Kiewra, Opening Repertoire: ...c6 (Everyman 2017); Sverre Johnsen and Torbjorn Ringdal Hansen, Win with the Caro-Kann; Milos Pavlovic, The Modernized Semi-Slav (Thinkers Publishing 2024). These are model plans written for this course; the full annotated games are in those books.

THE TRAPS YOU MUST AVOID:

1. ...dxc4 against 6.Qc2 before White commits the bishop. He recaptures with a pawn after b3 and the entire ...b5 plan disappears.
2. ...Bf5 in the English move order 1.c4 c6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nbd7, because 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 and the bishop must return to c8.
3. ...dxc4 against 5.Bg5 - that is the Botvinnik, and we avoid it with 5...h6 every single time.
4. ...c5 in the Meran before the rook and the b-pawn are ready. The break needs ...a6 or ...b4 first.

THE TRAPS YOU CAN SET:

1. The delayed capture. Against 6.Qc2, take on c4 only once the bishop must recapture. The same move is worthless on move six and excellent on move eight.
2. The ...b4 deflection. In the modern Meran, ...b4 before ...c5 drives the knight to a4 or e2, where it does far less.
3. The Exchange Slav ...Ne4 and ...f5. Most opponents assume symmetry means safety and never adjust.
4. The fork after 12.Nxe4 dxe4 in the Exchange - the pawn hits bishop and knight at once.

THE BRIDGE TO YOUR WHITE REPERTOIRE:
- The e5-outpost you build with White in the Colle is the outpost you deny with Black by playing ...Nd7 and ...f5.
- The Bxh7 sacrifice you hunt for with White is the one you defuse with ...h6 and ...Nf8.
- The isolated queen's pawn you attack in the Colle is the one you attack again in the Panov, from the same side of the board.

Teach the two colours together. A student who has seen a structure from both sides understands it roughly twice as fast as one who has only defended it.

FIRST, A WARNING YOU MUST NOT SKIP: White can now play 2.e4 and you are simply in a Caro-Kann. That is not a problem - it is your other course - but it does mean every student needs BOTH courses. Do not tell yourself "my opponent plays 1.d4, so I only need this one".

THE TRAPS YOU MUST AVOID:
1. ...dxc4 against 6.Qc2 before White commits the bishop. He recaptures with a pawn after b3 and the entire ...b5 plan disappears.
2. ...Bf5 in the English move order 1.c4 c6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nbd7, because 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 and the bishop must return to c8.
3. ...dxc4 against 5.Bg5 without knowing your ground - that is the Botvinnik, and we avoid it with 5...h6 every single time, entering the Moscow or Anti-Moscow instead.
4. ...c5 in the Meran before the rook and the b-pawn are ready. The break needs ...a6 or ...b4 first.
5. In the Anti-Moscow Gambit itself, 11...Ne6?? after the queen trade on d2 - it allows a forced mate in two with 12.Bb5+ and 13.Nxf7. A single careless retreat in a razor-sharp position is enough to lose outright; this whole chapter is a reminder of why.
THE TRAPS YOU CAN SET:
1. The delayed capture. Against 6.Qc2, take on c4 only once the bishop must recapture. The same move is worthless on move six and excellent on move eight.
2. The ...b4 deflection. In the modern Meran, ...b4 before ...c5 drives the knight to a4 or e2, where it does far less.
3. The Exchange Slav ...Ne4 and ...f5. Most opponents assume symmetry means safety and never adjust - and if White greedily grabs the pawn with an early Nxe4, the resulting queen trade and knight retreat leave Black with the bishop pair and the better ending.
4. The fork after 12.Nxe4 dxe4 in the Exchange - the pawn hits bishop and knight at once.
THE BRIDGE TO YOUR WHITE REPERTOIRE:
- The e5-outpost you build with White in the Colle is the outpost you deny with Black by playing ...Nd7 and ...f5.
- The Bxh7 sacrifice you hunt for with White is the one you defuse with ...h6 and ...Nf8.
- The isolated queen's pawn you attack in the Colle is the one you attack again in the Panov, from the same side of the board.
Teach the two colours together. A student who has seen a structure from both sides understands it roughly twice as fast as one who has only defended it.

WHERE WE ARE GENUINELY FINE:

WHERE WE MAKE A CONCESSION:
- Against 6.Bh4 we either accept a gambit that demands real study, or we decline and give White a comfortable game. There is no third road. Choose deliberately, and do not pretend the declining line is objectively equal - it is sound, not equalising.

WHERE THE THEORY MOVES FASTEST:
The Meran and the Moscow Gambit. If you take those up, expect to refresh them every year or two. The Exchange Slav, the Catalan set-up and the London lines will still be valid in ten years.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR HOW YOU SPEND YOUR TIME:
Put your study hours into the lines that do not expire, and use a reliable declining line in the ones that do - unless the sharp line is genuinely your style. A repertoire you maintain badly is worse than a slightly quieter one you know well.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES OF YOUR 1.d4 REPERTOIRE.

Most of your games leave theory around move fourteen. What decides them is whether you recognise the structure in front of you.

1. THE MERAN STRUCTURE (pawns a6-b5-c5 against White's centre).
Plan: ...Bb7, ...a6, then ...c5. After d4-d5 and the exchange on e6, use the f-file and think seriously about castling long.
Do not: hurry ...c5 before ...a6 - the break loses its force.

2. THE MOSCOW STRUCTURE (we own the bishop pair, no weaknesses).
Plan: ...g6 and ...Bg7, then ...e5 or ...c5 at the right moment.
Do not: rush. The bishop pair does not expire; improve a piece and wait.

3. THE DOUBLED g-PAWN STRUCTURE (after Nxg6 hxg6).
Plan: use the open h-file, and remember that f5 and h5 are permanently denied to White.
Do not: think of the doubled pawns as a weakness. You accepted them on purpose.

4. THE SYMMETRICAL EXCHANGE STRUCTURE.
Plan: ...Ne4 and ...f5, or a minority attack with ...b5-b4.
Do not: assume a draw.

THE HABIT TO BUILD: at move fourteen, before calculating anything, name the structure. Then play the plan.

THE BRIDGE TO YOUR WHITE REPERTOIRE: three of these four structures appear in the Colle course from the other side. The e5-outpost you build with White is the outpost you must deny with Black. The Bxh7 sacrifice you look for with White is the one you defuse with ...h6 and ...Nf8. Studying both colours of the same structure is the fastest way to understand it.

THE MERAN. White refuses to play a waiting move and sends the bishop straight to d3, and that choice has a hidden cost: it hands us a free tempo.
WHY WHITE ACCEPTS THIS: our knight already sits on d7 rather than developing further, and sooner or later we will need the move ...c5 to free our position. In White's mind, the tempo he gives away now with ...dxc4 he gets back later, when we "waste" a move on the c5 break. Keep that trade in mind - it is the logic behind the whole variation.

THE MERAN. Now our plan is fixed and easy to remember:
1. Take on c4 with tempo.
2. Play ...b5 to gain queenside space.
3. Put the bishop on b7, where it finally gets the long diagonal.
4. Break with ...c5 to open the position for our pieces.

That is four moves and one idea. Learn it and you will never be lost in this opening.

WHY WHITE ALLOWS THIS TEMPO LOSS: Lakdawala's own explanation is the clearest way to remember it. White's bishop move to d3 costs him a tempo now, on the understanding that Black will eventually need the move ...c5 to free his own position - handing the tempo straight back. Both sides are betting on the same break. The question is only who executes it better.

THE TEMPO TRADE THAT DEFINES THE WHOLE VARIATION: White spends a move getting his bishop to c4 only to see it kicked straight back with ...b5. Lakdawala's own framing of this exchange is the clearest way to hold it in your head - White is betting that Black's own coming ...c5 break will cost an equivalent tempo later, evening the account. Whether that bet pays off is decided by exactly the lines below.

THE MOSCOW VARIATION proper. White gives up the bishop pair for extra space and a small lead in development. Grandmaster Alexey Dreev, who has played this exact structure as Black dozens of times, sums up the whole idea in one sentence: White is betting that he can put his space and development to use before our two bishops start to matter. If he plays passively, he loses that bet.

THE STRUCTURE: we own the bishop pair and have no structural weaknesses at all. White has slightly more space and easier short-term piece play.

THE MODERN SYSTEM, in Dreev's own words - this is how he characterises White's choice at this exact juncture. From here Black has two genuinely different roads, and this is the single most important branching point in the whole variation.
BRANCH A: 11...h5!? Theory here is still comparatively undeveloped, which is either an opportunity or a warning depending on how you like your chess. Dreev's own assessment is that the resulting positions differ completely from the alternative below, and that there remains real room to find new ideas rather than just reciting known theory.
BRANCH B: 11...Bg7, the move Dreev describes as becoming very popular in recent years, and the one we recommend studying first, since it is the more principled and more thoroughly tested of the two. But be warned before you commit to it: White's sharpest try here, 12.Nxf7!?, is the exact piece sacrifice Topalov played against Kramnik at Wijk aan Zee 2008 - one of the most famous games in this entire opening. Kramnik did not defend accurately and lost brilliantly; the defence has since been improved, and Dreev's own verdict is that Black now has more than enough resources, but the theory of that one move is still actively developing and no final word has been spoken. The calmer alternative, 12.Nxd7, is not calm at all in practice - it leads directly to 12...Qxd7 13.Bd6!, a genuine wedge in Black's position where only the precise 13...a6! holds the balance; more natural-looking tries such as 13...e5?! walk into forced, only-move sequences that can lose outright within a handful of moves.
THE HONEST CONCLUSION, and it applies to every single branch of this chapter: there is no safe, simplified single line to memorise here the way there is almost everywhere else in this repertoire. Dreev's own book runs to some two hundred pages on this variation alone, packed with only-moves, novelties and improvements from year to year. The correct way to take this line up is to work through his book chapter by chapter with a board and an engine, treat every sharp position as something to verify rather than trust from memory, and keep 6...Be7 in your back pocket for any game where you cannot afford a theoretical accident. When it is worth it: when you meet 6.Bh4 often, when you need real winning chances with Black, and when you actually have the study time to put in. Not otherwise.

That is a topic for the Advanced course once you actually face it - for now, simply know that "we are not going to provoke it" does not mean "we would be lost if it came".

THIS COURSE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER THREE.

The opening courses tell you WHICH MOVES to play. This one tells you WHAT TO DO once the opening is over - which is where almost every game is actually decided.

THE PRINCIPLE: openings do not produce positions, they produce STRUCTURES. The Colle produces only five. Learn the plan for each structure and you will never again reach move 15 without knowing what to do.

THE FIVE STRUCTURES:
1. THE GREEK GIFT - the h7 sacrifice. Not really a structure but a recurring pattern you must recognise instantly.
2. THE ROOK LIFT - your rook swings to h4 and joins the attack.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - pawn on e5, knight support, kingside pawn storm.
4. THE ISOLATED PAWN - you play against it, or with it.
5. BISHOP PAIR VERSUS SPACE - the slow anti-Colle games.

HOW TO STUDY THESE GAMES:
Do not memorise the moves. Play through each game once, then close the file and ask yourself: what was White's plan, and what was the move that made it work? If you can answer that, you have got what you need.

Every game here was actually played. The commentary explains the PLAN, not the variations.

THIS IS THE BIG ONE. Twenty complete tournament games, chosen because every single one lands on a position from YOUR repertoire - the same c3 Colle-Koltanowski lines you already studied in Cursus 1-3. Nothing here is a random "Colle game found on the internet." Every game was checked move by move against the lines you were taught, and only kept if it matches.
WHY A WHOLE COURSE OF COMPLETE GAMES?
Opening theory tells you WHAT to play. Model games teach you HOW to play it - what the pieces are actually trying to do once the book moves run out, which plans work, which plans look good but do not, and what a real opponent does when things go wrong for him. You cannot get that from a variations tree. You can only get it from full games.
HOW THIS COURSE IS ORGANISED - the same opening tree logic as Cursus 4, but far bigger:
SECTION A - The main line and the Nc6 set-up (5 games)
SECTION B - The Nbd7 set-up and the Re1/Rxe4 recapture (6 games)
SECTION C - The Reversed Stonewall, against ...Be7 and ...b6 (4 games)
SECTION D - The Phoenix, 9.b4 (3 games)

Every lesson starts on move 1, exactly like the other courses, so ChessTempo folds everything into one giant opening tree. You do not need to remember which lesson is which - just play through them in order.

YOU ALREADY KNOW THE SETUP. This course is about the part that actually decides games: knowing WHICH plan fits WHICH structure, and when to switch.

THE FOUR STRUCTURES THIS OPENING PRODUCES:
1. ISOLATED QUEEN'S PAWN (IQP) - after e4 and the exchanges. You attack; you must not let the game reach a simple endgame.
2. HANGING PAWNS c4/d4 - more space, but two pawns to defend. Push d4-d5 at the right moment.
3. THE e5 WEDGE - after Ne5 and f4. You attack on the kingside with g4; Black counters on the queenside.
4. BISHOP PAIR VS SPACE - the anti-Colle lines with h3 and g4. Slow, positional, and your two bishops decide the endgame.

THE ONE DECISION THAT MATTERS MOST:
Does e4 work, or not?
- Black plays ...Nc6 and ...c5 → dxc5 first, then e4. (Lessons 01-06)
- Black plays ...Nbd7 → Re1 first, then e4, and take with the ROOK. (Lessons 07-08)
- Black plays ...b6 and ...Bb7, or a very solid ...Be7 → e4 is blunted. Switch to Ne5 and f4. (Lessons 09-10)

WHAT CHANGED SINCE THE SPEEDCOURSE:
Your opponents now defend. They will play ...h6 to stop the sacrifice, or trade pieces to kill your attack. This course teaches you what to do when the knockout punch is not available - which is most games from here on.

THE KEY MOVE OF THE WHOLE COURSE. Trade on c5 FIRST, then play e4.

WHY? Two reasons:
1. Black's pressure on your d4-pawn disappears.
2. His bishop lands on c5 where it does nothing, and your e4 push comes with tempo.

Players who skip this move and rush e4 usually get a worse position.

THE FORK IN THE ROAD. Everything up to here stays exactly as you already know it. Only move nine changes.

WEAPON 1: 9.e4 - the classical Koltanowski. Direct, attacking, and what you have played until now.
WEAPON 2: 9.b4 - the Phoenix. Positional, and objectively the harder nut for a prepared opponent.

WHY YOU NOW NEED A SECOND WEAPON:
Against accurate defence, 9.e4 gives White very little. Lessons 01 to 03 show you exactly where and how strong players neutralise it. That is not a reason to abandon 9.e4 - below 1800 it still scores heavily - but you should know its limits rather than discover them in a tournament.

WHAT 9.b4 ACTUALLY IS:
A Semi-Slav with colours reversed and a tempo extra. That framing, which comes from Lakdawala, is the most useful thing to know about it. If you have ever played or faced the Semi-Slav, you already understand the plans: expand on the queenside, break with c3-c4, and use the majority.

THE CATCH, and be honest about it: your extra tempo is Bd3, and that bishop can become a target for ...e5-e4 and ...Ng4-e5. The tempo is not free.

HOW TO CHOOSE AT THE BOARD:
- Opponent unknown or under 1800 → 9.e4. Play for the attack.
- Opponent clearly prepared, or plays 9...Qc7 and 10...h6 confidently → 9.b4. Take him out of book into a slow game.
- You need a win with less risk → 9.b4. The structures are unbalanced without being sharp.

THE DECISION POINT. Here is how to think about it.

PLAY 9.e4 WHEN:
- Your opponent is under roughly 1800, or unknown.
- He has already played a slightly passive move (...Be7, ...Re8 early, ...Nbd7 setups).
- You want a sharp game and the initiative.
- You need to win and are willing to take some risk.

PLAY 9.b4 WHEN:
- Your opponent looks prepared, or confidently answers 9.e4 Qc7 10.Qe2 with 10...h6.
- You want an unbalanced game with less concrete risk.
- You are the stronger player and want a long game with many chances to outplay him.
- You are facing someone who has clearly studied your games. This is your surprise weapon - use it sparingly and it stays one.

A WORD OF CAUTION ON REPERTOIRE BUILDING:
Do not try to play both in the same tournament game. Decide before you sit down. The worst outcome is knowing two systems shallowly instead of one deeply.

My recommendation for most students: master 9.e4 completely first. Add 9.b4 only once you are consistently reaching the middlegames from Lessons 01 to 03 and finding them unsatisfying. That is the signal you have outgrown the classical line - and not a day before.

T.Hillarp Persson - L.Karlsson, Swedish Championship, Gothenburg 2006.

THE BEST DEFENCE, and what every well-prepared opponent plays. It takes g5 away from your knight and removes the sacrifice from the position permanently.

THE POINT OF THIS GAME: Black spends a tempo to rule out any future Greek gift on h7. It is a completely reasonable idea and you will meet it often - but it is not free. Compare this directly to the sacrifice lessons from Cursus 1-2: taking away one sacrifice does not win the game on its own, and it can even hand White a fresh target on h6 instead.

White switches straight to reversed-Semi-Slav mode rather than forcing the issue with an immediate e4-e5. This is the same territorial idea behind the 9.b4 Phoenix you will meet later in Section D, just arriving one move later via a different route.

SUMMARY: 10...h6 removes one sacrifice, not the whole attack. If Black spends a tempo defusing the Greek gift, look for the queenside break with b4 and c4 instead - the reversed Semi-Slav plan behind the Phoenix works here too.
L.Pecot - A.J.Tavares, correspondence 1998.
